questions.q: Per this lesson, where do most real-world encryption failures actually occur?
options: In how the key is handled across its lifetime, not in the underlying cryptographic math
Only in the choice of programming language used
Encryption failures are almost always caused by network latency
In the mathematical algorithms themselves, which are usually broken
questions.explain: The lesson states the cryptography is sound; failures come from mishandling the key — poor storage, no rotation, over-sharing, or loss.

questions.q: What is the most common real-world key management gap identified in this lesson?
options: Using an HSM instead of a software-based key store
Rotating keys too frequently for no reason
Generating too many keys for a single system
Skipping key rotation — a key generated once and never touched again means a single leak compromises everything forever
questions.explain: Without rotation, there's no limit on the exposure window if a key is compromised at any point without anyone knowing.

questions.q: In the DEK/KEK key hierarchy pattern, what is the data-encrypting key (DEK) responsible for?
options: Protecting the key-encrypting key from exposure
Storing backup copies of the database schema
Doing the actual, high-volume work of encrypting the data itself
Authenticating users logging into the database
questions.explain: The KEK's only job is protecting the DEK; the DEK does the high-volume encryption work, and rotating the DEK is cheaper than re-encrypting everything under a brand-new top-level key.

questions.q: What makes a hardware security module (HSM) different from storing a key in a config file or environment variable?
options: An HSM is simply a software library with no physical component
An HSM stores keys in plaintext for faster access
An HSM is only used for storing passwords, never encryption keys
The key material never leaves the HSM in plaintext form — operations are sent to the device instead of exporting the key
questions.explain: Because the raw key material is never extractable from an HSM, it can't be stolen the way a key sitting in a config file or environment variable can.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say that who holds a key is a segregation-of-duties question?
options: Segregation of duties has no relevance to key management
Only auditors are allowed to generate encryption keys
A key custodian who can also access the data the key protects effectively has unrestricted access, making the encryption add no real barrier for that person
Key custodians are legally required to also be database administrators
questions.explain: Splitting key-custodian duties from the people who query the encrypted data day to day means no single compromised account defeats the whole encryption scheme.
